title: The reported total sample size
published: To study fact-checking during the 2020 election season, we conducted eight preregistered panel experiments (total [[N = 17,681]]).
corrected: To study fact-checking during the 2020 election season, we conducted eight preregistered panel experiments (total [[N = 17,629]]).
note: The article's own appendix Table 1 reports the eight panel sizes as 2,321, 2,090, 2,059, 2,390, 2,582, 2,200, 1,599 and 2,388, which sum to 17,629, and the deposited respondent data hold exactly that many.

title: The count of experiments in which misinformation reduced accuracy
published: Overall, exposure to the misinformation significantly decreased accuracy in [[twelve]] out of the twenty-four opportunities.
corrected: Overall, exposure to the misinformation significantly decreased accuracy in [[thirteen]] out of the twenty-four opportunities.
note: Appendix Table 1 prints all thirteen in its unadjusted rows, and the deposited estimates and the reproduction agree on every one of them.

title: The persistence percentages in the main text were not recomputed when the analysis was revised
published:
We show that [[66 per cent]] of the initial effect of fact-checks on factual beliefs is still detectable one week after initial exposure, with [[50 percent]] detectable after more than two weeks.

The effects of fact-checks observed immediately after treatment dissipate somewhat from Wave 1 to Wave 2, on average, at [[66.4 per cent]] of the initial magnitude.

On average, the effect in Wave 3 is [[50 per cent]] the magnitude of the original effect, though the smaller number of issues and subjects increases our uncertainty.

The effects of fact-checks persisted at [[66 per cent]] the original magnitude after one week and at [[50 per cent]] after more than two weeks.
corrected:
We show that [[48.9 per cent]] of the initial effect of fact-checks on factual beliefs is still detectable one week after initial exposure, with [[34.3 percent]] detectable after more than two weeks.

The effects of fact-checks observed immediately after treatment dissipate somewhat from Wave 1 to Wave 2, on average, at [[48.9 per cent]] of the initial magnitude.

On average, the effect in Wave 3 is [[34.3 per cent]] the magnitude of the original effect, though the smaller number of issues and subjects increases our uncertainty.

The effects of fact-checks persisted at [[48.9 per cent]] the original magnitude after one week and at [[34.3 per cent]] after more than two weeks.
note:
The Wave 3 correction is larger than the change of pooling alone would make it. The deposited three-wave models fitted with covariates regress the wrong outcomes, so the ratio behind appendix Table 7's 0.43 instruments the Wave 2 outcome rather than the Wave 3 outcome. Refitted on Wave 3, the random-effects pool is 34.3 per cent with covariates and 38.9 per cent without them.

One caveat the correction does not remove. A random-effects pool is still a precision-weighted average: it weights each fact-check by how precisely that fact-check's ratio was measured, not by how much of the population of fact-checks it stands for. The corrected percentages are therefore still not quite the quantity the sentences describe, which is how much of a typical fact-check's effect survives a week. They are the figures the article should have reported, and they are the ones a reader can check against the appendix; treating them as an estimate of the population average asks more of them than a precision-weighted average can give.
